exampleAnswers.title: Evaluating an Expression Involving Special Angles in Degrees

question.explanation:
Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

  • Let's first consider the angle $45^\circ.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle $45^\circ$ corresponds to the point \[ \left(\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2},\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2} \right). \] Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have \[ \sin 45^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}.\]

  • Now, let's consider the angle $30^\circ.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle $30^\circ$ corresponds to the point \[ \left(\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2},\dfrac{1}{2} \right). \] Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have \[ \cos 30^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}. \]

Finally, we combine the results:

\begin{align*} \sin 45^\circ +\cos 30^\circ &= \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{align*}

example.title: Evaluating an Expression Involving Special Angles in Degrees

question.explanation:
Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

Let's first consider the angle $315^\circ.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle $315^\circ$ corresponds to the point $\left(\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2},-\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2} \right).$ Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\sin{315^\circ} = -\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}.$

Now, let's consider the angle $150^\circ.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle $150^\circ$ corresponds to the point $\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2},\dfrac{1}{2} \right).$ Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\cos{150^\circ} = -\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}.$

Finally, we combine the results:

\begin{align*} \sin^2\left(315^\circ\right) + \cos{150^\circ} &= \left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)^2 + \left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2} -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}(1-\sqrt{3}). \end{align*}

example.title: Evaluating an Expression Involving Special Angles in Degrees

question.explanation:
Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

  • Let's first consider the angle $60^\circ.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle $60^\circ$ corresponds to the point \[ \left(\dfrac{1}{2},\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2} \right). \] Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have \[ \cos 60^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}.\]

  • Now, let's consider the angle $90^\circ.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle $90^\circ$ corresponds to the point \[ \left(0,1 \right). \] Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have \[ \sin 90^\circ =1. \]

Finally, we combine the results:

\begin{align*} \cos 60^\circ - \sin 90^\circ &= \dfrac{1}{2} - 1 \\[5pt] &=-\dfrac12 \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Evaluating an Expression Involving Special Angles in Radians

question.explanation:
Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

Let's first find the value of angle $2\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ where $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}.$

\[ 2\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)+\dfrac{\pi}{2}=\dfrac{7\pi}{6}. \]

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\dfrac{ 7\pi}{6}$ corresponds to the point $\left( -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, -\dfrac{1}{2} \right).$ Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\cos\left( \dfrac {7\pi} {6}\right) = -\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}.$

Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\sin\left( \dfrac {7\pi} {6}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{2}.$

Using the fact that $\cot{\theta} = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}$ and $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$ we have \begin{align*} \cot\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right) &= \dfrac{\cos\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right)}{\sin{\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right) }} = \dfrac{\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2}\right)}{\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)} = \sqrt{3},\\[5pt] \tan\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right) &= \dfrac{\sin{\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right) }}{\cos{\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right) }} = \dfrac{\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)}{\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}. \end{align*}

Finally, we combine the results:

\[ \cot\left(2\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) + \tan\left(2\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \cot\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right) + \tan\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right) =\sqrt 3+ \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3} = \dfrac{4\sqrt{3}}{3}. \]

example.title: Evaluating an Expression Involving Special Angles in Radians

question.explanation:
Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

Let's consider the angle $\dfrac{\pi}{4}.$ From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ corresponds to the point $\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right).$ Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\cos\left( \dfrac {\pi} {4}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2}.$

Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\sin\left( \dfrac {\pi} {4}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.$

Using the fact that $\sec\theta=\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}$ and $\cot{\theta} = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta},$ we have \begin{align*} \sec\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) &= \dfrac{1}{\cos{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) }} = \dfrac{1}{\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)} = \sqrt 2,\\ \cot\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) &= \dfrac{\cos{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) }}{\sin{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) }} = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)} = 1. \end{align*}

Finally, we combine the results:

\[ \sec\left(\dfrac \pi 4\right) + \cot\left(\dfrac \pi 4\right) = \sqrt{2}+1. \]
